segments.translit: siddhācāryo hi sarahapādas tam evārthaṃ bhāvasvarūpāvagamāt lokārthāya vadati—
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha}, having understood the [true nature]{svarupa} of things, speaks that same meaning for the good of the world:
segments.note: Munidatta opens by saying that the [siddha]{siddha} master [Saraha]{p-saraha} (a siddha is an accomplished tantric adept), having understood the [true nature]{svarupa} of things, speaks 'that same meaning' for the good of the world (cp.39.m1): a formula he uses to open other songs too.

flags.note: 'That same meaning' (tam evārtham) is not specified: presumably the teaching already set out in the songs before this one; Munidatta does not say which (cp.39.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees word for word (don de nyid dngos po'i ngo bo nyid rtogs nas 'jig rten pa'i ched du gsungs so).

segments.translit: suiṇem ityādi | bho nijamana(ṇa) cittarā[ja] tavāvidyādoṣāt sadrūpāvagamakatvāt svapne 'pi dravyābhilāṣ[ā]t guruvacanenduraśmayas trailokye sphāritāḥ | ataḥ kutra sthāne tvayā sthātavyaṃ bho cittarāja |
segments.translation: '[Dream]{svapna}' and so on. O my own [mind]{citta}, [king of mind]{king-of-mind}: this comes from your fault, [ignorance]{avidya}, since it makes things known as real, and from longing for things even in a [dream]{svapna}. The moonbeams of the [guru]{guru}'s word have spread through the [three worlds]{trailokya}. So in what place are you to stay, O [king of mind]{king-of-mind}?
segments.note: Munidatta calls the mind '[king of mind]{king-of-mind}' and traces the [dream]{svapna} to its fault, [ignorance]{avidya}, which makes things seem real (cp.39.m2). The [guru]{guru}'s word spreads its moonbeams through the [three worlds]{trailokya}: where can the mind stay? He does not gloss [ghuṇḍa]{ghunda}, a word of uncertain sense; his 'O king of mind' stands in its place.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) cites the lemma as stong nyid ('emptiness'), as its line 1a reads (perhaps suṇṇa for suiṇa), yet its comment goes on to speak of a dream (rmi lam gyi rjes la yang, 'even after a dream'), so the dream survives in the Tibetan comment (cp.39.m2). It also differs elsewhere: 'the faults of ignorance and the rest' (ma rig pa la sogs pa'i nyes pa rnams) for 'your fault, ignorance'; 'because they are understood as having the nature of what is not bliss' (bde ba ma yin pa'i ngo bor rtogs pa'i phyir), with a negative, for sadrūpāvagamakatvāt, 'since it makes things known as real'; a simile with no Sanskrit counterpart (dper na lha thams cad lag tu rnam par brkyang ba bzhin dang gnyid sad pa bzhin du, 'as all the gods stretched out in the hand, and as on waking from sleep'); and, before the moonbeams, 'now, by the power of the Buddha's merit' and 'my true guru' (bdag gi bla ma dam pa), with 'thoroughly illuminated' (rab tu gsal ba) for 'spread' (sphāritāḥ). The translation follows the Sanskrit.

On 1b (cp.39.m2): Munidatta cites neither bihārem̐ nor ghuṇḍa. 'The moonbeams of the guru's word have spread (sphāritāḥ) through the three worlds' stands where the song has gurubaaṇa bihārem̐re, so he seems to take bihāra- as the word's ranging or spreading everywhere, which fits the draft's 'roams'; the Tibetan line has spyod lam, 'conduct, deportment', a usual rendering of vihāra. His closing vocative 'O king of mind' stands where the song has ghuṇḍa: at most he took it as an address to the mind, and he gives it no sense. He also renders kaise, 'how', as kutra sthāne, 'in what place', where the draft has 'how will you stay'; the Tibetan comment agrees with him (gnas gang du), its line with the draft (ji lta bu).

The first sentence has three ablatives (tavāvidyādoṣāt, sadrūpāvagamakatvāt, dravyābhilāṣāt) and no main verb. 'This comes from' is supplied, taking them as Munidatta's account of the dream of 1a; they could instead give the reason for the next sentence, the guru's word spreading because of the mind's faults (cp.39.m2).

The lemma is cited as suiṇem (suiṇe- before ityādi), and the paraphrase has svapne 'pi, 'even in a dream', as if from a locative suiṇe, where the song has suiṇā. nijamana(ṇa) carries Shastri's parenthesis, apparently the manuscript's spelling, and cittarā[ja] his restoration (cp.39.m2).

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ draḍhayati—
akaṭetyādi | ākaṭaḥ [56ka] āścaryaṃ | gurupādapadmaprasādāl līlayā mayāvagato 'si | hūṅkāra(ro) bījodbhava(vā) bho cittarāja | gaaṇeti prabhāsvare praviṣṭo 'si idānīṃ avidyādoṣavināśakaukṛtyaṃ bhagnaṃ tava |
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes that same meaning firm.
'A [wonder]{adbhuta}' and so on. Ākaṭa means a marvel. By the [grace]{prasada} of the [guru]{guru}'s [lotus]{lotus} feet I have come to know you in [play]{lila}, O [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, born from the seed, the syllable [hūṃ]{hum}. 'In the [sky]{gagana}': you have entered [clear light]{prabhasvara}. Now your [remorse]{kaukrtya} at the ruin wrought by the fault of [ignorance]{avidya} is broken.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as Saraha telling the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, born from the seed-syllable [hūṃ]{hum}, that he knows it by the [guru]{guru}'s grace; 'in the sky' means it has entered [clear light]{prabhasvara}, and its [remorse]{kaukrtya} is broken (cp.39.m3). He cites gaaṇa, 'sky', for the edition's aṇā, and says nothing of the wife in [Baṅga]{pl-banga}.

equations.en: clear light (prabhāsvara), which the king of mind has entered

flags.note: The compound avidyādoṣavināśakaukṛtyam is obscure: literally 'fault-of-ignorance-destruction-remorse'. 'Your remorse at the ruin wrought by the fault of ignorance' is a guess. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ma rig pa'i skyon sna tshogs pa 'gyod pa bcom pa, 'the various faults of ignorance, remorse, are destroyed', with sna tshogs pa, 'various', where the Sanskrit has vināśa, as if reading vividha; that would give 'your fault of ignorance and manifold remorse are broken'. Its line 2b also has sna tshogs pa for biṇāṇā, perhaps hearing nānā, 'various', in it (cp.39.m3).

Munidatta gives no gloss of biṇāṇā (cp.39.m3). His last sentence follows 2b word for word, idānīṃ for pare, bhagnaṃ for bhāgela, tava for tohāra, so the remorse compound stands where the song has biṇāṇā: he seems to take it as the remorse that ignorance brings. Nothing in the segment supports or rules out the draft's 'consciousness' (vijñāna); the Tibetan line has g.yo sgyu sna tshogs pa, 'various deceits'.

Nothing in the segment answers to baṅge jāyā nilesi, 'you took a wife in Baṅga': Munidatta passes over it (cp.39.m3). 'You have entered clear light' is his gloss on 'in the sky', not on the wife, and the Tibetan comment is silent too.

Munidatta cites gaaṇeti, 'sky', where the edition's 2a has aṇā, and the Tibetan line and comment both have nam mkha' la, 'in the sky'; this supports the draft's emendation to gaaṇā (cp.39.m3). hūṅkāra(ro) bījodbhava(vā) is read, with the Tibetan (hUM yig sa bon las byung ba), as a vocative compound, 'born from the seed, the syllable hūṃ'; the parentheses seem to give the manuscript's nominative forms.
The folio mark [56ka] stands inside the gloss (ākaṭaḥ [56ka] āścaryaṃ). It is Shastri's note of the manuscript leaf, kept in the transliteration and not translated.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenādhimātrasatvasyānuśaṃsām āha—
adaa ityādi | bhavasatvasya hi moho 'yam adbhutaḥ | yasmād ātmasvaraparāparabhedavibhāgaṃ sa paśyati | ata eva sāhaṅkāreṇa manasi paramārthacittasyodayas tava nāstīti | (syodayātavanīti) |
tathā cāgamaḥ | sāhaṅkāre manasi viśamaṃ yāji janmaprabandho
nāhaṅkāyaś calati hṛdayād ātmadṛṣṭau tu satyāṃ |
nānyaḥ śāstā jagati jayino nāsti nai[rā]tmavādī
nānyas tasmād upaśamavidhes tatmatād asti mārgaḥ ||
tattvavidāṃ pratīre nīrendvā(ndrā)didvādaśadṛṣṭāntadvāreṇa bhavet sarvaśūnyapramāṇo[pa]pannā siddhir bhavatīti |
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [praise]{anusamsa} of the being beyond measure.
'A [wonder]{adbhuta}' and so on. For this [delusion]{moha} of the being in [existence]{bhava} is a [wonder]{adbhuta}, since he sees things divided by the distinction of [self and other]{sva-para}, of other and not-other. For this very reason, while the mind has I-making, the arising of the [ultimate]{paramartha} [mind]{citta} does not take place for you.
And so the [scripture]{agama}:
While the mind has I-making, the chain of [birth]{janma} runs an uneven course;
I-making does not stir from the [heart]{hrdaya} while the view of a self is present.
There is no teacher in the [world]{jagat} but the Victor, no other who teaches [selflessness]{nairatmya};
so there is no [path]{marga} to the practice of calming other than his teaching.
On the shore of those who know [reality]{tattva}, by way of the [twelve examples]{dvadasa-drstanta} beginning with the [moon in water]{udakacandra}, [accomplishment]{siddhi} comes about, established by the [valid cognition]{pramana} of the [emptiness]{sunyata} of all.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as the wonder of worldly [delusion]{moha}: the being in existence sees self split from other, and while the mind holds to 'I' the ultimate mind cannot arise (cp.39.m4). A scripture verse backs this; he adds that through twelve examples, the [moon in water]{udakacandra} first, those who know reality gain accomplishment by proving all empty.

citations.quoted: sāhaṅkāre manasi viśamaṃ yāji janmaprabandho … nānyas tasmād upaśamavidhes tatmatād asti mārgaḥ
citations.work: Not named: Munidatta introduces it only as āgama, 'scripture'; not identified here

flags.note: adhimātrasatva: adhimātra, 'beyond measure', can mean 'of the highest degree' or 'intense, excessive'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems can shin tu chen po, 'very great being', which suits 'praise' (rjes su bsngags pa); but the comment describes the delusion of the worldly being, so the praise may be ironic, or 'beyond measure' may refer to the delusion. 'The being beyond measure' keeps both open (cp.39.m4).

ātmasvaraparāparabhedavibhāgam is obscure: svara may be a slip for sva, and parāpara may mean 'other and not-other' or 'far and near'. Rendered 'the distinction of self and other, of other and not-other'. The Tibetan has rang dang gzhan dang pha rol tu 'byed pa'i rnam par dbye ba, 'dividing into self, other and the far side' (cp.39.m4).

'…syodayas tava nāstīti' is Shastri's correction; his parenthesis gives the manuscript's (syodayātavanīti). The Tibetan has khyod len par byed do, 'you take it up', with no negative, which may reflect the manuscript's wording rather than Shastri's nāsti. The Sanskrit also mixes cases (sāhaṅkāreṇa manasi), rendered 'while the mind has I-making' after the verse's sāhaṅkāre manasi (cp.39.m4).

The verse is corrupt in print, and the translation reads: viṣamaṃ, 'uneven, wrong', for viśamaṃ (the Tibetan mi bzang, 'not good', agrees, though na śamaṃ, 'does not come to rest', would also scan and give easier sense); yāti for yāji; nāhaṅkāraś for nāhaṅkāyaś; tanmatād, 'than his teaching', for tatmatād (or tvanmatād, 'than your teaching', if the verse addresses the Buddha). The Tibetan diverges in line 2: 'free of pride, beings are then free of the view of a self in the mind' (nga rgyal dang bral 'gro ba yang / sems la bdag lta de nas bral) (cp.39.m4).

The last sentence is partly corrupt: pratīre, 'on the shore' (of those who know reality), is odd and may stand for pratīte, 'when it is understood'; bhavet … bhavati doubles the verb. The Tibetan treats the sentence as four more lines of the verse (ending ces so) and has skye ba med la sgrub por byed, 'accomplishes in non-arising', where the Sanskrit has bhavet and siddhir bhavati (cp.39.m4).

Munidatta does not name the water bubble of 3b, nor the innate: his twelve examples beginning with the moon in water presumably include images like the bubble, and 'the emptiness of all' answers to suṇa apaṇā, 'empty in itself' (cp.39.m4).

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena caturthāna[nda]m ātmāha—
amiam ityādi | sahajajāna[nde] sthite sati rūpādiviṣa[ya]vip[ā]ka[n] [57] prasahy[ai]va harasi | bho karmeva vaśyacitta vicāraka | gṛham iti svakaṃ kāyaṃ pīnakam iti | rāgadveṣamohādikaṃ samūhaṃ tava nijagṛhiṇījñānamudrānairātmāṃ samāliṅgya tasya bhakṣaṇaṃ niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ mayā kartavyam |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—gharaṇiñe paraviṣa khajjai ityādi |
gharavito khajjai saṅgi rajjai ṇaṭho rāa verāaṇī |
akula ṇaddhī cittā bhaṭṭī joiṇī so patidāsa ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [greatness]{mahatmya} of the four [joys]{ananda}.
'[Nectar]{amrta}' and so on. While [innate joy]{sahajananda} is present, you seize by force the ripened fruits of the [sense objects]{visaya}, [form]{rupa} and the rest, O [mind]{citta} in the power of [action]{karma}, O [examiner]{vicara}! '[House]{house}' means one's own [body]{body}. 'Pīnaka.' The host of [passion]{raga-passion}, [hatred]{dvesa}, [delusion]{moha} and the rest: having embraced your own [wife]{grhini}, the [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, I am to eat it, that is, make it [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}.
And so [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha}: 'The housewife eats another's [poison]{visa}', and so on.
The householder is eaten, the companion delights, passion and dispassion are lost;
bound to the kinless, the mind fallen away, the [yoginī]{yogini}: she is her lord's servant.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the couplet as the greatness of the four joys (with the Tibetan): with [innate joy]{sahajananda} present, the mind still seizes [sense objects]{visaya} (cp.39.m5). The [house]{house} is one's own body. Embracing one's own wife, the [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra} ('wisdom seal') [Nairātmā]{nairatma} ('selfless one'), the speaker must eat the host of passion, hatred and delusion: make it without intrinsic nature.

citations.work: Saraha (Munidatta names Sarahapāda); perhaps his Dohākoṣa

citations.quoted: gharavito khajjai saṅgi rajjai ṇaṭho rāa verāaṇī | akula ṇaddhī cittā bhaṭṭī joiṇī so patidāsa
citations.work: Unattributed; apparently the continuation of the Saraha quotation (absent from the Tibetan); perhaps Saraha's Dohākoṣa

flags.note: The opening tṛtīyapadena caturthāna[nda]m ātmāha is corrupt (literally something like 'the fourth joy, self, he says'). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dga' ba bzhi'i bdag nyid che ba gsungs, 'he states the greatness of the four joys', as if from caturānandamāhātmyam āha, and the translation follows it. If caturtha-, 'fourth', is original, read 'the greatness of the fourth joy' (cp.39.m5).

rūpādiviṣa[ya]vip[ā]ka[n] [57] prasahy[ai]va harasi is damaged and restored by Shastri; his viṣa[ya] is 'object', not viṣa, 'poison'. The Tibetan has gzugs la sogs pa yul gyi dug ji ltar spyod par byed, 'how do you consume the poison of objects, form and the rest?', with both 'object' and 'poison', as a question, and nothing for vipāka, 'ripening', or prasahya, 'by force'. sahajajāna[nde] is read sahajānande with the Tibetan (lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba); the extra ja looks like a repetition (cp.39.m5).

harasi can mean 'you take away, remove' as well as 'you seize'; with 'remove' the sentence would praise the mind for clearing away objects once innate joy is present. 'You seize' is chosen because 4a reproaches the mind for swallowing poison beside nectar, and the Tibetan asks how one could consume the poison of objects. His paraphrase puts innate joy where the song has nectar, without an explicit gloss (cp.39.m5).

bho karmeva vaśyacitta vicāraka: karmeva may be karma iva, 'as it were action', karmaiva, or a slip for karmavaśya-; rendered 'O mind in the power of action'. The Tibetan has las kyi dbang phyug, 'lord of karma', as if reading vaśin or īśvara for vaśya. For the draft's 4a pasara basa: vaśya- answers to basa, 'power, control', which supports 'in the power of'; nothing in the comment clearly renders pasara, 'what is spread out'. The Tibetan line has gzhan dbang, 'in another's power', as if reading para-vaśa (cp.39.m5).

pīnakam iti follows 'house means one's own body' with no explanation. In the order of 4b it stands where the edition has pārem̐ (the draft's 'far shore'), so it may be Munidatta's citation of that word in another form, its gloss lost; or it may describe the body ('the plump one', from pīna). The Tibetan comment joins it to the body as rang gi lus kyi btung ba can, 'having the drink of one's own body', and its line 4b has btung ba, 'drink', at that point (cp.39.m5).
tava, 'your', may go with samūham ('your host of passion…') or with nijagṛhiṇī ('your own wife'); the Tibetan takes the second (khyod kyi rang gi khyim mi mo), and so does the translation (cp.39.m5).

On 4b mare: Munidatta's paraphrase has no verb of killing. mayā kartavyam, 'is to be done by me', answers to mai … khāiba, 'I will eat', and the gerund in his sentence is samāliṅgya, 'having embraced', which does not render mare. So his wording does not decide between 'having killed' and 'me'; the Tibetan line (bdag ni ma rungs gnyen 'dun za, 'I eat the bad kin') has no killing either (cp.39.m5).

The Apabhraṃśa couplet gharavito khajjai … so patidāsa follows the quoted line of Saraha in the Sanskrit but is absent from the Tibetan, which closes the quotation with ces pa la sogs pas so. Its text is garbled and the translation is tentative: verāaṇī may be vairāgiṇī, 'the woman free of passion'; akula ṇaddhī may be 'bound to the kinless' or corrupt; cittā bhaṭṭī may be 'the mind fallen away' or 'the lady Mind'; patidāsa may be 'her lord's servant' or a corrupt verb (cp.39.m5).

Where the Sanskrit has bhakṣaṇa, 'eating', of the host of passions, the Tibetan has btung ba, 'drinking' (de'i btung ba ni rang bzhin med par bdag gis byed pa'o), in keeping with the btung ba of its line 4b (cp.39.m5).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena svacchandacaryām āha | sarahapādasiddhācāryo hi vadati | saraha bhaṇa ityādi | duṣṭa baladam iti | duṣṭaviṣayaṃ balaṃ dadāti iti duṣṭabalada cittarājo bodhavyaḥ | ekena tena duṣṭena trailokyaṃ nāśitaṃ | tena duṣṭabaladena mayā kiṃ kartavyam | go iti indriyaṃ | tasya sālambanaṃ svakāyaṃ taṃ śūnyaprabhāsvararūpaṃ kṛtvā guruvacanaprasādāt svacchandena trijagati viharaṇaṃ karomi iti |
tathā ca śāntidevapādāḥ—
sva[57ka]cchandacaryānilaya ityādi || 39 ||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states [conduct]{carya} [at will]{svacchanda}. For the [siddha]{siddha} master [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha} says: '[Saraha]{p-saraha} says' and so on. 'Bad ox' (duṣṭa balada): because it gives (dadāti) strength (bala) to bad (duṣṭa) [objects]{visaya}, it is the [bad ox]{dusta-balada}; it is to be understood as the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}. By that one bad one alone the [three worlds]{trailokya} were destroyed. What am I to do with that [bad ox]{dusta-balada}? Go, 'cow', means the [senses]{indriya}. Having made their support, one's own [body]{body}, into the form of empty [clear light]{prabhasvara}, by the [grace]{prasada} of the [guru]{guru}'s word I roam [at will]{svacchanda} in the [three worlds]{trailokya}.
And so the venerable [Śāntideva]{p-santideva}: 'Whose abode is [conduct]{carya} [at will]{svacchanda}…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta calls the couplet [conduct]{carya} [at will]{svacchanda}. The [bad ox]{dusta-balada}, 'what gives strength to bad objects', is the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, which alone destroyed the three worlds; go, 'cow', means the [senses]{indriya} (cp.39.m6). Having made their support, one's own body, empty [clear light]{prabhasvara} by the guru's grace, Saraha roams the three worlds at will.

equations.en: the king of mind (cittarāja), so called because it gives strength (balaṃ dadāti) to bad objects

citations.work: Śāntideva (Munidatta names Śāntidevapāda); perhaps the Bodhicaryāvatāra

flags.note: On 5b's subject: Munidatta's instrumental ekena tena duṣṭena, 'by that one bad one', makes the bad ox, the king of mind, the destroyer of the world; the first person enters only with 'I roam at will'. For his reading this decides the question in favour of the draft's 'Alone it destroyed the world', though it does not settle the grammar of the Bengali. The Tibetan comment agrees (gcig pu de yis ma rungs 'jig rten gsum 'joms pas) (cp.39.m6).

For go iti indriyam, 'go means the senses', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has go zhes pa ni glang po'o, 'go means the ox'. For duṣṭaviṣayaṃ balaṃ dadāti it has 'because it gives the strength of bad objects' (ma rungs pa yul gyi stobs ster ba'i phyir), and it transcribes the word (duSh+Ta ba la da) (cp.39.m6).

Munidatta does not gloss bara, 'better', or suṇa, 'empty', in 5a. His support of the senses, one's own body, made into the form of empty clear light seems to take the empty cowshed as the body, with śūnya answering to suṇa, but he does not say so (cp.39.m6).

svacchandacaryānilaya can be divided -caryā-nilaya, 'whose abode is conduct at will' (so the Tibetan, rang gi 'dun pas spyod pa'i gnas), or -caryā-anilaya, 'conduct at will, homeless'. Munidatta names only Śāntideva; that the phrase is from the Bodhicaryāvatāra is a guess. The folio mark [57ka] inside the word and the closing song number are not translated (cp.39.m6).

proposals.definition: Śāntideva, the Indian Buddhist author to whom the Bodhicaryāvatāra is ascribed. Munidatta names him, with the honorific -pāda, for a phrase on conduct at will (svacchandacaryā) at the end of his comment on song 39 (cp.39.m6); the Tibetan has zhi ba lha'i zhabs. Not Śāntipāda, the poet of song 15.
proposals.rationale: Named by Munidatta at cp.39.m6. The glossary has his Bodhicaryāvatāra (tx-bodhicaryavatara) but no entry for the person, and the name is easily confused with Śāntipāda (p-santi).

questions: 2b biṇāṇā: Munidatta has kaukṛtya, 'remorse', at that point (cp.39.m3), and the Tibetan line has g.yo sgyu sna tshogs pa, 'various deceits'. Neither supports the draft's 'consciousness'. Keep it with a flag, or reconsider the line?

4a pasara basa: Munidatta's vocative vaśyacitta, 'mind in the power (of action)' (cp.39.m5), and the Tibetan line's gzhan dbang, 'in another's power', both take basa as 'power', and the Tibetan points to para-vaśa. Would 'in another's power' serve better than the draft's 'in the power of what is spread out'?
4b pārem̐, the draft's 'far shore': Munidatta has an unexplained pīnakam at that point (cp.39.m5) and the Tibetan line has btung ba, 'drink'. Is 'far shore' still the reading to keep?
4b mare: neither Munidatta's paraphrase (cp.39.m5) nor the Tibetan line has a verb of killing. Keep 'I will kill and eat', or consider reading mare as 'me'?
The opening of cp.39.m5 is translated from the Tibetan ('the greatness of the four joys'), as instructed. Would you rather print the Sanskrit's 'fourth joy' and leave the Tibetan to the flag?
1b: Munidatta paraphrases kaise, 'how', as 'in what place' (cp.39.m2), and the Tibetan comment agrees. Worth a note beside the draft's 'how will you stay'?

Equations: I left the term empty for the plain lexical gloss ākaṭa = āścarya (cp.39.m3), so that it is not filed as a symbolic reading of adbhuta, and for eating = making without intrinsic nature (cp.39.m5), which has no entry. The glossary shows Munidatta reading eating this way elsewhere too (the crocodile, cp.02.m2). Should eating get an entry?

The Apabhraṃśa couplet that follows Saraha's line in cp.39.m5 (gharavito … patidāsa) is garbled and its translation is tentative; it is not in the Tibetan. Can it be checked against an edition of Saraha's dohās?
I proposed p-santideva for Śāntideva, named in cp.39.m6, to keep him apart from Śāntipāda (p-santi).
